key_points: Shaft excavation drives horizontal pressures toward active values; outward structural loading drives them toward passive.
Horizontal arching becomes significant at depths exceeding two shaft diameters.
Arching coefficient λ = circumferential stress / vertical stress; ranges from 1 (Terzaghi 1943) down to K0.
Cheng et al. (2007) solution (Figure 4-12) provides radial stress for λ = 1 and λ = K0.
If rigid top bracing prevents active state development, design horizontal pressures may reach at-rest (plane strain) values.
Detailed earth pressure guidance in DM 7.2.
sections.applicability: Applies when calculating earth pressures on vertical cylindrical shaft walls in coarse-grained soil, accounting for horizontal arching at depth.

sections.title: Shafts in Clay
sections.summary: Provides the formula for critical depth zcrit in clay, above which no lateral support is needed for a vertical shaft. The critical depth is zcrit = 2su / γt, where su is undrained shear strength and γt is total unit weight. This equation defines the self-supporting zone near the ground surface in clay shaft excavations.
sections.body:
No support is needed from the ground surface to a depth of zcrit for shafts in clay. The critical depth (zcrit) is:

zcrit = 2su / γt

where:
su = the undrained shear strength of the soil and
γt = the total unit weight of the soil.
key_points: In clay, no lateral shaft support is needed from the surface down to the critical depth zcrit.
Critical depth zcrit = 2su / γt, where su is undrained shear strength and γt is total unit weight.
Below zcrit, lateral support must be provided to maintain shaft stability.

equations.description: Critical depth for unsupported clay shaft: zcrit = 2su / γt, where su is undrained shear strength and γt is total unit weight of soil. Defines the depth above which no lateral support is required.

sections.applicability: Applies when determining the depth above which no lateral support is needed for a vertical shaft excavated in clay soil.

sections.title: Numerical Solutions for Stresses in Soil
sections.summary: Introduces numerical methods for evaluating stresses in soil as a complement to analytical and chart-based solutions. Explains that computer programs and finite element/finite difference methods are essential for handling complex subsurface profiles and loading conditions that exceed the limitations of closed-form elastic solutions.
sections.body:
The analytical and chart-based solutions presented in this chapter are an excellent starting point for evaluation of stresses within a soil mass. However, their applicability is limited by the constraints and assumptions of each. These methods also struggle to effectively model complex subsurface profiles and loading conditions.

Computer programs and numerical solutions are an important part of geotechnical engineering practice. This section provides a brief overview of the application of numerical methods to the evaluation of stresses.
key_points: Analytical and chart-based solutions are useful starting points but are limited by their assumptions and cannot easily model complex subsurface profiles or loading conditions.
Numerical methods (finite element and finite difference) are widely used in geotechnical engineering for stress evaluation.
Finite element method (FEM) is somewhat more popular than finite difference for stress analysis problems.
Calculation of accurate stresses via FEA is relatively straightforward; accurate deformation prediction requires significantly more expertise.
sections.applicability: Applies when analytical or chart-based stress solutions are insufficient due to complex geometry, loading, or subsurface conditions.

sections.title: Numerical Analysis Types
sections.summary: Surveys the types of numerical analysis programs used for stress evaluation in geotechnical engineering. Covers elastic-solution-based programs (Settle3D, CONSOL, SETOFF) for consolidation settlement and continuum-based methods (FEM and FDM). Notes the FEM is more popular for stress analysis; both methods divide soil/rock into elements governed by constitutive laws and failure criteria.
sections.body:
Some computer programs (e.g., Settle3D, CONSOL, SETOFF) are available that directly rely upon elastic solutions, such as those presented in this chapter, to calculate changes in stress. These programs are specifically formulated for the solution of consolidation settlement problems discussed in the next chapter. The benefit provided by these programs is the automated calculation of changes in stress and the ability to consider time-dependent changes. However, the solutions depend on the same assumptions as the elastic solutions on which they are based.

Many continuum-based numerical analysis techniques are available. The most common of these in geotechnical engineering are the finite element and finite difference methods, with the former being somewhat more popular for stress analysis problems. These approaches divide the soil or rock into elements or grid points. The relationships between the external and gravitational forces acting on the elements (or grid) and the corresponding displacements are defined using constitutive (stress-strain) laws and failure criteria.

The following sections provide a condensed overview focused on the calculation of stresses using the finite element method. The use of finite element analysis (FEA) to determine stresses is relatively straight-forward. Calculation of accurate deformations requires significantly more expertise and experience. For a practical introduction to the use of FEA in geotechnical engineering see Bradley and VandenBerge (2015). A more in-depth perspective can be found in the books by Potts and Zdravkovic (1999, 2001).
key_points: Programs such as Settle3D, CONSOL, and SETOFF use elastic solutions to automate stress change calculations, particularly for consolidation settlement.
These elastic-solution-based programs share the same assumptions and limitations as the underlying closed-form solutions.
FEM and FDM are the dominant continuum-based numerical methods in geotechnical engineering.
FEM is somewhat more popular than FDM for stress analysis problems.
Stress calculation via FEA is relatively straightforward; deformation prediction requires significantly more expertise.
Key references: Bradley & VandenBerge (2015) for practical FEA intro; Potts & Zdravkovic (1999, 2001) for in-depth treatment.
sections.applicability: Applies when selecting an appropriate numerical analysis approach for stress or consolidation problems in geotechnical engineering.

sections.title: Linear Elastic Stress Analysis
sections.summary: Describes the application of linear elastic constitutive theory in FEA for stress analysis. For a single-material model, stresses are independent of elastic modulus E; when multiple materials are present, relative E values affect stress distribution due to arching. Required input parameters are only E and Poisson's ratio ν (or equivalent elastic constants).
sections.body: The simplest FE analyses use linear elastic constitutive theory, which relates changes in stress linearly to strains (or displacements). For a linear elastic analysis, the only required material parameters are the elastic modulus, E, and Poisson's ratio, ν (or any other two elastic constants such as shear modulus or bulk modulus). For problems with only one material type (and one value of E), the calculated stresses will be independent of the value of E selected. However, when more than one material type is present, the relative values of E assigned to each material in the analysis can impact the calculated stresses because of arching and similar phenomena.
key_points: Linear elastic FEA requires only two material parameters: elastic modulus E and Poisson's ratio ν.
For single-material problems, calculated stresses are independent of the chosen value of E.
When multiple material types are present, relative E values affect stress distribution due to arching and similar phenomena.
Linear elastic analysis is the simplest FEA approach but is only strictly valid over small strain ranges.
sections.applicability: Applies when performing the simplest form of FEA for stress analysis in geotechnical problems with one or more soil/rock material types.

sections.title: Nonlinear Elastic Stress Analysis
sections.summary: Covers nonlinear constitutive models for soil stress analysis, focusing on the Duncan-Chang hyperbolic model. Explains the model's four key observations about stress-strain behavior and summarizes its parameters (K, n, Rf, Kb, m, Kur). Notes that linear elastic analysis is typically within 10% of nonlinear results for embankment principal stresses, per VandenBerge et al. (2014).
sections.body:
The stress-strain behavior of geological materials is truly linear over only a small range of strains. A properly selected nonlinear constitutive model will provide a more accurate prediction of behavior but will require additional input parameters and expertise. VandenBerge et al. (2014) found that major principal effective stresses calculated for embankments with linear elastic analysis were typically within 10% of the values calculated using more rigorous and time-consuming nonlinear procedures.

One of the earliest and most common nonlinear constitutive theories for soil is the hyperbolic model proposed by Duncan and Chang (1970) and described in more detail in Duncan et al. (1980). This model can also consider stress dependent variations in Poisson's ratio (or bulk modulus). It can be used with either effective stress (drained) or total stress (undrained) problems, provided the model parameters are determined using the appropriate type of test.

The Duncan-Chang model is based on the following observations:
• The principal stress difference (σ1 – σ3) tends to vary in a hyperbolic manner with strain,
• The initial modulus (Ei) increases with increased confining stress in a manner that can be described by a power function,
• The ultimate value of (σ1 – σ3) predicted by the hyperbola tends to be greater than the value measured by the test,
• The bulk modulus (Bt) of soil increases with increased confining stress in a manner that can be described by a power function.

Soil tends to respond in a stiffer, approximately linear manner with modulus (Eur) when unloaded and reloaded after some amount of shearing. The required parameters are summarized and illustrated in Table 4-13 and Figure 4-13.
key_points: Geological materials behave linearly only over a small strain range; nonlinear models are needed for more accurate predictions.
Linear elastic analysis of embankments typically yields major principal effective stresses within 10% of nonlinear results (VandenBerge et al. 2014).
The Duncan-Chang hyperbolic model (1970) is one of the most common nonlinear constitutive models for soil.
Key model observations: (σ1–σ3) follows a hyperbolic stress-strain curve; Ei and Bt increase with confining stress as power functions.
The model can be applied to both drained (effective stress) and undrained (total stress) problems.
Parameters K, n, Rf, Kb, m, and Kur govern the model; soil is stiffer during unload-reload with modulus Eur.
See Table 4-13 for parameter summary and Figure 4-13 for illustration.

sections.applicability: Applies when performing nonlinear FEA of soil stress-strain behavior, particularly for embankments and problems where stress-dependent stiffness is important.

sections.title: Numerical Modeling Best Practice
sections.summary: Provides guidelines for achieving consistent and accurate stress predictions in finite element analysis of geotechnical problems. Recommends use of isoparametric elements, uniform meshes, appropriate aspect ratios (≤5), small element sizes (1–2% of domain height), and inclusion of boundary water pressures. Based on findings from VandenBerge et al. (2014).
sections.body:
Both linear and nonlinear finite element analysis can be used to make accurate predictions of stresses. The following guidelines have been found to yield the most consistent and uniform stress predictions (VandenBerge et al. 2014).

• Use isoparametric elements (i.e., 8-noded rectangles or 6-node triangles).
• Use a uniform mesh with elements of approximately the same shape, especially within any zones of interest.
• Use elements with an appropriate aspect ratio, preferably longest to shortest dimension, less than or equal to five.
• Keep the element size as small as practical with respect to the overall dimensions. A maximum element height of approximately 1 to 2% of the height of the problem domain is preferred.
• Remember to include the boundary water pressures from any impounded water present in the model.
key_points: Use isoparametric elements: 8-noded rectangles or 6-node triangles for best stress predictions.
Maintain a uniform mesh with consistent element shapes, especially in zones of interest.
Element aspect ratio (longest to shortest dimension) should be ≤ 5.
Maximum element height should be approximately 1–2% of the total problem domain height.
Always include boundary water pressures from impounded water in the model.
sections.applicability: Applies when setting up finite element models for geotechnical stress analysis to ensure accurate and consistent results.

sections.title: Initial or Geostatic Stresses
sections.summary: Explains how initial (geostatic) stress states are established in FE models. Vertical stresses develop from gravity loading; horizontal stresses tend toward K0 conditions. For linear elastic models K0 = ν/(1−ν). Discusses how to handle initial deformations (numerical artifacts), and how to model overconsolidated conditions (K0 > 1.0) by load-unload cycling.
sections.body:
The initial stress state in a FE model is dependent on the process used to "turn on" gravity and stress within the model. Vertical stresses are governed mostly by gravity loading. As the mesh deforms in response to gravity, horizontal stresses will develop and tend toward at rest (K0) conditions for a level, laterally-constrained mesh. For a linear elastic model, the value of K0 will be equal to ν / (1-ν). Calculation of initial horizontal stresses in this manner will yield correct results, and K0 will be less than 1.0, which is always the case for primary loading. The calculation of initial horizontal stresses in this way will lead to initial deformation of the model and the layer thicknesses may no longer match the in situ conditions. These displacements are a numerical artifact and should be zeroed or removed prior to examining the effects of new loading conditions. Overconsolidated conditions with K0 greater than 1.0 can be modelled by loading and then unloading the model, following the process by which K0 > 1.0 conditions occur in nature.

In many cases, the details of the initial stress process are program specific. The engineer using FEA should become familiar with the various options available so that appropriate methods are applied.
key_points: Vertical stresses in FE models are governed by gravity loading; horizontal stresses develop toward K0 conditions in level, laterally-constrained meshes.
For linear elastic models, K0 = ν / (1 − ν), which is always less than 1.0 for primary loading.
Initial deformations from gravity loading are numerical artifacts and must be zeroed before applying new loads.
Overconsolidated conditions (K0 > 1.0) can be modeled by simulating loading followed by unloading.
Initial stress procedures are program-specific; engineers must understand the options available in their software.
sections.applicability: Applies when establishing initial or geostatic stress conditions in finite element models for geotechnical analysis.

sections.title: Staged Construction or Stress History
sections.summary: Describes the use of staged finite element analysis to model construction sequencing, geologic stress history, and element addition/removal. Staged models are essential for nonlinear analysis where material properties vary with stress level, and are required for predicting displacements around excavations and tunnels. For stress-only analysis, staging is unnecessary in linear elastic models.
sections.body:
Finite element analysis allows the sequence of loading and construction staging to be modeled numerically. To a lesser extent, geologic stress history can also be modeled. Within the model, this occurs by adding and subtracting elements (or their weight) in steps. Staged models are especially important for nonlinear analysis because the properties of the material change with stress level.

For example, a staged approach is required to predict stresses and displacements around open excavations and tunnels. The initial ground conditions should be modeled after which the effects of removing soil or rock can be considered.

For cases where only stress distributions are required, such staging is unnecessary in linear elastic analysis. The use of a staged model is required, even for linear elasticity, to predict correct patterns displacement.
key_points: Staged FEA models construction sequencing and geologic stress history by adding/removing elements in steps.
Staging is critical for nonlinear analysis because material properties vary with stress level.
A staged approach is required for modeling open excavations and tunnels (initial ground → element removal).
For linear elastic analysis, staging is not needed for stress distributions only, but IS required for correct displacement patterns.
Geologic stress history can be partially modeled through staged loading and unloading.
sections.applicability: Applies when using FEA to model construction sequences, excavations, tunnels, or geologic stress history in geotechnical problems.

sections.title: Evaluation of Stress Due to Applied Loads
sections.summary: Explains how to use staged FE models to evaluate stress changes from applied loads. The initial stage(s) establish in situ conditions; new loads (distributed, point, or soil layers) are added in subsequent stages; stress changes are computed by differencing results between stages. Emphasizes checking FEA results against analytical solutions and notes 2D vs. 3D limitations for different foundation geometries.
sections.body:
Changes in stress due to applied loads can be evaluated using a staged FE model. The first stage(s) of the model are used to create the desired initial state of stress that best represents the in situ conditions. At this point, the new loading can be added to the model in various forms, including distributed loads, point loads, and new soil layers. The predicted changes in stress can then be evaluated by comparing the predicted stress at convenient points within the model between subsequent stages. Where possible, the changes in stress predicted by FE models should be checked with analytical solutions such as those presented earlier in this chapter.

Engineers should be aware of the limitations of their numerical analyses. For example, two-dimensional FEA are useful for predicting changes in stress below long foundations, embankments, and large area fills because such problems can be analyzed in a plane strain manner. However, a three-dimensional program would be required to predict changes in stress below more complex conditions, such as a rectangular foundation.
key_points: Use staged FE models: first stage(s) establish initial in situ stress; subsequent stages add applied loads (distributed, point, or new soil layers).
Stress changes are evaluated by differencing predicted stresses between model stages.
Always check FEA stress predictions against available analytical solutions.
2D (plane strain) FEA is appropriate for long foundations, embankments, and large-area fills.
3D FEA is required for stress changes beneath complex geometries such as rectangular foundations.
sections.applicability: Applies when using staged FEA to evaluate stress changes from applied loads in geotechnical engineering problems.

sections.title: Evaluation of Stress within Embankments and Slopes
sections.summary: Addresses the added complexity of calculating stresses in slopes and embankments where no closed-form solution exists and K0 conditions do not prevail. Recommends modeling natural slopes by starting with level ground in FEA and progressively excavating elements to form the slope geometry, using multiple analysis stages to establish correct initial stress conditions.
sections.body:
The calculation of stresses is more complex for slopes and embankments compared with relatively level ground. First, no closed-form analytical solution is available for comparison because the soil in a slope is not laterally restrained. The lack of lateral restraint also means that K0 conditions will not be present, especially close to the face of a slope.

Stresses near natural slopes are best evaluated by starting with level ground in the FE model and progressively removing (excavating) elements to form the slope. Multiple stages of analysis may be required to establish the initial conditions. The removal of elements mimics the process by which the slope was formed in nature.
key_points: No closed-form analytical solution exists for stresses in slopes or embankments due to lack of lateral restraint.
K0 (at-rest) conditions do not prevail near slope faces due to the absence of lateral constraint.
Model natural slope stresses by starting with level ground in FEA and progressively removing elements to form the slope.
Multiple analysis stages may be needed to establish correct initial stress conditions for slopes.
Element removal mimics the natural geologic process of slope formation.
sections.applicability: Applies when evaluating stresses within slopes, embankments, or other geometries that lack lateral restraint and cannot be analyzed using closed-form solutions.

Each entry cites a specific authoritative publication for further study.
